==Problem==

Emily sees a ship traveling at a constant speed along a straight section of a river. She walks parallel to the riverbank at a uniform rate faster than the ship. She counts <imath>210</imath> equal steps walking from the back of the ship to the front. Walking in the opposite direction, she counts <imath>42</imath> steps of the same size from the front of the ship to the back. In terms of Emily's equal steps, what is the length of the ship?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }70\qquad\textbf{(B) }84\qquad\textbf{(C) }98\qquad\textbf{(D) }105\qquad\textbf{(E) }126</imath>

==Solution 1 (One Variable)==
Let <imath>x</imath> be the length of the ship.
Then, in the time that Emily walks <imath>210</imath> steps, the ship moves <imath>210-x</imath> steps.
Also, in the time that Emily walks <imath>42</imath> steps, the ship moves <imath>x-42</imath> steps.
Since the ship and Emily have the same ratio of absolute speeds in either direction, <imath>\frac{210}{210-x} = \frac{42}{x-42}</imath>. Dividing both sides by <imath>42</imath> and cross multiplying, we get <imath>5(x-42) = 210-x</imath>, so <imath>6x = 420</imath>, and <imath>x = \boxed{\textbf{(A) }70}</imath>.

~ihatemath123

==Solution 2 (Two Variables)==
Let the speed at which Emily walks be <imath>42</imath> steps per hour. Let the speed at which the ship is moving be <imath>s</imath>. Walking in the direction of the ship, it takes her <imath>210</imath> steps, or <imath>\frac {210}{42} = 5</imath> hours, to travel. We can create an equation: <cmath>d = 5(42-s),</cmath> where <imath>d</imath> is the length of the ship. Walking in the opposite direction of the ship, it takes her <imath>42</imath> steps, or <imath>42/42 = 1</imath> hour. We can create a similar equation: <cmath>d = 1(42+s).</cmath> Now we have two variables and two equations. We can equate the expressions for <imath>d</imath> and solve for <imath>s</imath>:
<cmath>\begin{align*}
210-5s &= 42 + s \\
s &= 28. \\
\end{align*}</cmath>
Therefore, we have <imath>d = 42 + s = \boxed{\textbf{(A) }70}</imath>.

~LucaszDuzMatz (Solution)

~Minor edits by Yvz2900

== Solution 3 (Three Variables) ==
Suppose that Emily and the ship take steps simultaneously such that Emily's steps cover a greater length than the ship's steps.

Let <imath>L</imath> be the length of the ship, <imath>E</imath> be Emily's step length, and <imath>S</imath> be the ship's step length. We wish to find <imath>\frac LE.</imath>

When Emily walks from the back of the ship to the front, she walks a distance of <imath>210E</imath> and the front of the ship moves a distance of <imath>210S.</imath> We have <imath>210E=L+210S</imath> for this scenario, which rearranges to <cmath>210E-210S=L. \hspace{15mm}(1)</cmath> When Emily walks in the opposite direction, she walks a distance of <imath>42E</imath> and the back of the ship moves a distance of <imath>42S.</imath> We have <imath>42E=L-42S</imath> for this scenario, which rearranges to <cmath>42E+42S=L. \hspace{19.125mm}(2)</cmath>
We multiply <imath>(2)</imath> by <imath>5</imath> and then add <imath>(1)</imath> to get <imath>420E=6L,</imath> from which <imath>\frac LE = \boxed{\textbf{(A) }70}.</imath>

~Steven Chen (www.professorchenedu.com)

~MRENTHUSIASM

==Solution 4 (Using the Boat's "Step")==
Every time Emily takes a step, the boat also "takes a step". Call the length of the boat's step <imath>s</imath>. Call the length of the boat <imath>x</imath>.
 
When Emily is walking in the same direction as the boat, every time she takes a step the boat moves an additional distance of <imath>s</imath>. This means that she travels a total distance of <imath>x + 210 s</imath> to reach the other end of the boat.
 
When Emily is walking in the opposite direction of the boat, every time she takes a step the distance till the end of the boat reduces by <imath>s</imath> (since the boat is coming towards her and moves a distance of <imath>s</imath>). This means that she travels a total distance of <imath>x - 42 s</imath> to reach the other end of the boat. 

Taking Emily's step as a unit of distance, we now have two equations 
<cmath>\begin{align*}
210 &= x + 210 s, \\
42 &= x - 42s.
\end{align*}</cmath>
Solving for <imath>x</imath> you get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }70}</imath>.

~zeeshan12

== Solution 5 (Relative Speeds) ==
Call the speed of the boat <imath>v_s</imath> and the speed of Emily <imath>v_e</imath>.

Consider the scenario when Emily is walking along with the boat. Relative to an observer on the boat, her speed is <imath>v_e-v_s</imath>.

Consider the scenario when Emily is walking in the opposite direction. Relative to an observer on the boat, her speed is <imath>v_e+v_s</imath>

Since Emily takes <imath>210</imath> steps to walk along with the boat and <imath>42</imath> steps to walk opposite the boat, that means it takes her <imath>5</imath> times longer to walk the length of a stationary boat at <imath>v_e-v_s</imath> compared to <imath>v_e+v_s</imath>.

This means that <imath>5(v_e-v_s)=v_e+v_s</imath>, so <imath>v_s = \frac{2v_e}{3}</imath>.

As Emily takes <imath>210</imath> steps to walk the length of the boat at a speed of <imath>v_e- \frac{2v_e}{3}=\frac{v_e}{3}</imath>, she must take <imath>\frac13</imath> of the time to walk the length of the boat at a speed of <imath>v_e</imath>, so our answer is <imath>\frac{210}{3} = \boxed{\textbf{(A) }70}</imath>.
